name: Sargunalingeswarar Temple, Tirukkarukkudi (Marudhanallur)
deity: Shiva as Sargunalingeswarar (Karukudi Nathar), a swayambhu sand lingam, with the goddess Advaita Nayaki (Sarvalankara Nayaki)
period: Tevaram era (hymned 7th century); later Chola structural temple
summary: Marudhanallur, the Tevaram's Tirukkarukkudi, near Kumbakonam, honours Shiva as Sargunalingeswarar — worshipped as a swayambhu lingam of sand — with the goddess Advaita Nayaki, 'the lady of non-duality.' A Paadal Petra Sthalam hymned by Tirugnana Sambandar, it keeps a wealth of legend: Rama worshipping before his march to Lanka, a Pandyan king named Sargunan, and Brahma's own worship here.

sections.history: Marudhanallur, whose Tevaram name is Tirukkarukkudi, lies about 5–6 km south of Kumbakonam, past Sakkottai on the way to Valangaiman, in Thanjavur district. It is a Paadal Petra Sthalam, hymned by Tirugnana Sambandar, counted among the Shiva shrines on the southern bank of the Kaveri. The stone temple is of the Chola period and later; its inscriptions are mostly illegible or lost, so its recorded history is slight, but its legends are rich.
sections.architecture: A Dravidian delta temple, the shrine enshrines Sargunalingeswarar — also called Karukudi Nathar and Brahmapureeswarar — in the sanctum, with the goddess Advaita Nayaki, also Sarvalankara Nayaki and Kalyani Ambica, in her own shrine. The presiding lingam is a swayambhu lingam of sand, a manal-lingam, which is bathed with special care; a Nandi and the parivara devatas complete the plan.
sections.legends: The temple keeps several legends. By one, Rama worshipped Shiva here before his march to Lanka, asking Hanuman to bring a lingam from the north — a motif that binds the place to the great Ramayana shrines. By another, a Pandyan king named Sargunan worshipped the lord here, giving the deity the name Sargunalingeswarar. Brahma too is said to have worshipped at this spot, whence the lord is also called Brahmapureeswarar. The sand lingam marks the lord as swayambhu, self-manifest, a form of special sanctity.
sections.festivals: The temple observes Maha Shivaratri in Masi (February–March), Navaratri in Purattasi (September–October) and the Mondays of Karthikai, with Pradosha worship, at the quiet scale of a village shrine near Kumbakonam. Pilgrims on the Paadal Petra trail of the southern Kaveri include Marudhanallur among their stops.
sections.experience: At Marudhanallur the pilgrim meets a self-manifest lord of sand, worshipped since the days of Rama and Brahma. Before Sargunalingeswarar and Advaita Nayaki — whose name itself speaks of the oneness beyond all duality — the visitor finds a quiet Kaveri-bank shrine whose layered legends reach from the Ramayana to the Tevaram.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Marudhanallur (Tirukkarukkudi) is about 5–6 km south of Kumbakonam, past Sakkottai on the way to Valangaiman, in Thanjavur district. Kumbakonam is the nearest major rail head, with frequent buses and taxis to the village.
